issues.explanation: Occupation 'Retired' is implausible for age 28 (retired is implausible if age < 50).

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits awkwardly with 'my memories are very clear and detailed' and 'mostly pictures or images' for a PTSD profile tied to a life-threatening accident; this pattern suggests unusually easy verbal processing despite vivid intrusive-style memory, which weakens coherence of the memory node.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The threat item about repeatedly checking whether someone is following him implies an interpersonal pursuit/assault-type danger theme, which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being a life-threatening accident and with the rest of the profile, which does not otherwise indicate persecution-related threat.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: 'I dwell on what other people have done to me' also implies an interpersonal harm/blame theme that does not fit well with the accident trauma context or the other selected appraisals, memories, and threats.

issues.item: Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
issues.explanation: Restricting food as a coping strategy is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other items describe accident-related sensory threat (loud sounds, startle), image-based trauma memory, and self-critical appraisals, with maladaptive responses centered on avoidance/removal from reminders and rumination/meaning seeking. Undereating introduces a qualitatively different coping pattern that is not reflected elsewhere in Triggers, Threat, Memory, or Negative Appraisals, making it the least clinically coherent item in this five-component profile.

Clinical Vignette: Marco

Marco was fifty-two when the accident happened, and he had spent thirty years building a reputation as a meticulous, unflinching director—the kind of professional who could hold a vision steady through fourteen-hour days and temperamental crews. He had won awards. He had made films that people remembered. His partner, David, had learned long ago that Marco's work was not separate from his identity; it was woven through him so completely that there was no distinguishing the man from the artist.

The accident occurred during a night shoot in an abandoned warehouse in New Jersey. Marco had insisted on minimal lighting to capture a particular quality of shadow for a pivotal scene. He was standing on a raised platform, directing the gaffer on a final adjustment, when the platform's support beam—corroded, unnoticed—gave way beneath him. He fell fifteen feet onto concrete, his left leg fracturing in two places, his ribs cracking, his head striking the edge of a metal crate. The darkness that had seemed so essential to his artistic vision became the darkness in which he lay bleeding, unable to call out, unable to move, certain for the minutes before someone found him that he was dying alone in the dark.

Three months into his recovery, Marco returned to work. The physical wounds had healed into scars. But something else had fractured and had not mended. Darkness became intolerable to him. He could not sit through a screening in a dark theater without his chest tightening, his breath becoming shallow. He began requiring that all his sets be lit, even scenes meant to feel shadowed—he would direct cinematographers to create darkness through color grading rather than through actual absence of light. His crews noticed. His producers noticed. The artistic vision that had defined his work became constrained by something he could not name and could not control.

The hypervigilance arrived in layers. Unexpected sounds—a door slamming on set, the sudden blare of a speaker, a car horn outside the editing suite—would send a spike of adrenaline through his body. His hands would shake. He would startle visibly, something he had never done before, something he found humiliating. He had become the kind of person who jumped at ordinary noises, and he was acutely aware of how this appeared to others: weak, unstable, not himself.

The memories of the fall came to him primarily as images—the moment of the beam shifting, the sensation of weightlessness, the concrete rushing toward him—but he could not construct them into a coherent narrative. When David would ask him gently what had happened, Marco would find himself unable to articulate it. The experience existed in him as fragmented visual impressions and bodily sensations, not as a story he could tell.

What frightened him most was what he had become in response. He was a man who now avoided darkness, who flinched at sounds, who could not work the way he once had. He spent hours in distraction, scrolling through his phone, reorganizing his office, anything to avoid the thought that kept returning: Why did this happen to me? The question circled endlessly without answer. He had come to believe that his reactions since the accident—the fear, the hypervigilance, the inability to function as he once did—proved something fundamental about him: that he was not equipped to handle adversity, that he was inadequate in ways he had never suspected. The person he saw reflected back at him from David's concerned eyes was someone he no longer recognized.

Six months ago, Marco had stepped back from directing. He told his agent it was temporary. It was not temporary. Last week, after David found him sitting in the dark basement—not by choice, but because he had been testing himself and failed—Marco finally called a trauma therapist. He was terrified that no one could help him return to who he had been, and equally terrified that if he could not, there was nothing left of him worth saving.
